denver.overview: Denver's market is exhibiting stability and improving fundamentals across all sectors. The re-balancing from the oversupply perspective is a common theme. Submarkets outside Downtown Denver are leading the recovery — Cherry Creek Class A office and prime buildings lead new lease volumes, reflecting overcome return-to-office uncertainty. Industrial demand is blooming as a broadening set of tenants show interest, with 3PLs, aerospace, and advanced manufacturing emerging. The cyclical trough of multifamily has finally passed, with occupancy rising and little pipeline to slow the recovery.
headwinds: Office: New development staying dormant — just 1% of new inventory over the past 2 years
Office: Class B and C owners unwilling to invest in CIPs or offer competitive TI allowances will continue to face occupancy pressure
Industrial: Landlords prioritizing retention over new tenant pursuits, holding the market under equilibrium
tailwinds: Office: Tenants have overcome return-to-office uncertainty, promoting longer-term commitments
Office: Quality-concentrated demand on Class A
Industrial: Investors entering new supply-constrained submarkets, investing on upside market improvement
Multifamily: Widening performance gap between newer and dated properties — quality and location carry high value for disposition strategy

sourceReport.label: CBRE: Denver 2026 U.S. Real Estate Market Outlook — Midyear Review (PDF)

chicago.overview: Chicago's story is bifurcation, not decline. Trophy and new-build towers in Fulton Market and the West Loop are absorbing tenants at the expense of aging Loop office stock, some of which is heading toward functional obsolescence rather than recovery. Multifamily stays a steady, unglamorous performer — Chicago's relative affordability keeps renter demand consistent even without dramatic population growth. Industrial around O'Hare and the I-55/I-80 corridors continues to lean on the city's position as a national distribution hub. The bigger overhang across every asset class isn't fundamentals, it's the city and Cook County's fiscal and property-tax picture, which shows up as a valuation discount more than a demand problem.
headwinds: Office: Flight-to-quality is hollowing out older Loop stock, pushing vacancy and shadow space higher for anything short of top-tier
Multifamily: Rising property taxes and insurance costs are compressing NOI even where rent growth is healthy
Citywide: Ongoing city/county fiscal uncertainty is a persistent drag on investor sentiment and cap rates
tailwinds: Industrial: Rail and highway connectivity keep Chicago a top-tier national distribution hub with durable demand
Multifamily: Limited new supply relative to renter demand is keeping occupancy and rent growth resilient in most submarkets
Office: Fulton Market/West Loop trophy towers are still capturing outsized leasing activity — quality gets funded even in a down market

sourceReport.label: CBRE: Chicago 2026 U.S. Real Estate Market Outlook — Midyear Review (PDF)

miami.overview: Miami has been one of the strongest multifamily and office markets nationally, riding sustained in-migration, no state income tax, and a growing finance presence. That same growth has produced a wave of new multifamily supply in Brickell and Downtown that's now pressuring rent growth and pushing concessions up after several very strong years. Industrial stays structurally tight given how little developable land is left. Office picked up real momentum from financial-services relocations, but is now digesting new supply of its own rather than running purely on scarcity.
headwinds: Multifamily: Heavy new supply delivering in Brickell/Downtown is pushing concessions higher and slowing rent growth
Citywide: Insurance and climate risk (flood, hurricane) are structurally raising operating costs across every asset class
Industrial: Land scarcity is pushing land and construction costs up, making new development harder to underwrite
tailwinds: Office: Continued relocation of financial-services firms and family offices from the Northeast keeps trophy office demand resilient
Multifamily: In-migration and no state income tax keep supporting long-term demand even as new supply digests
Industrial: Port access and limited available land keep existing industrial stock structurally undersupplied

sourceReport.label: CBRE: South Florida 2026 U.S. Real Estate Market Outlook — Midyear Review (PDF)

sanfrancisco.overview: San Francisco's office market has been the poster child for post-pandemic distress, with vacancy near historic highs — though there are early, tentative signs of stabilization as AI-sector hiring pulls tenants back into the market, concentrated around the SoMa AI cluster. Multifamily has held up better than office, benefiting as renewed tech hiring brings workers back into the city. Lab/life-science space is the market's own soft spot, overbuilt relative to the current biotech venture-funding environment. The bigger picture: San Francisco's talent density and venture capital concentration are unmatched, which is exactly why it's positioned to benefit disproportionately if this AI-driven demand wave continues.
headwinds: Office: Vacancy remains near record highs, and older or poorly located buildings face real risk of long-term obsolescence or conversion
Life sciences/lab space: Overbuilt relative to the current venture-funding environment, leaving significant sublease and shadow vacancy
Citywide: High cost of doing business and lingering downtown perception issues continue to weigh on investor sentiment
tailwinds: Office: AI-sector leasing is the first genuine positive demand driver downtown office has seen since the pandemic
Multifamily: Renewed tech hiring tied to AI is bringing workers back into the city, supporting occupancy and rent growth
Long-term: Unmatched talent density and venture capital concentration position SF to benefit disproportionately from the next growth cycle

sourceReport.label: CBRE: San Francisco 2026 U.S. Real Estate Market Outlook — Midyear Review (PDF)
